requirements.requirement: Node1 provides a working POST /upload endpoint on TCP port 8080, reachable from node2.
requirements.summary: Node2 successfully reached node1:8080 and received expected HTTP responses. The service was enabled, listening, firewall-accessible, and remained operational after node1 reboot.

requirements.requirement: Raw request bodies up to and including 65536 bytes are accepted, with each upload stored in a separate byte-identical file under received/.
requirements.summary: Distinct 31-byte and 65536-byte requests returned 200 with different receipt names. The corresponding files had the exact client-side sizes and SHA-256 digests.

requirements.requirement: Bodies larger than 65536 bytes are rejected with HTTP 413 before a receipt is published.
requirements.summary: A 65537-byte request returned 413. Starting with one receipt, only the two accepted requests added files; no receipt or staging file appeared for the oversized request.

requirements.requirement: An interrupted request leaves no completed receipt.
requirements.summary: A connection declaring 65536 bytes was closed after sending 133 bytes and received HTTP 400. The completed-receipt count remained three and staging was empty afterward.
Both GET and POST requests to /other returned 404, and the same behavior was observed before and after reboot.

requirements.requirement: The pre-existing receipt in /srv/legacy2/http-upload-size-boundary is preserved.
requirements.summary: received/prior.bin remained 28 bytes with its original SHA-256 digest and ownership through testing and reboot.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on RHEL 7.9 with kernel 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64. The implementation ran successfully using the installed Python 2.7.5 runtime.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied by direct behavior and final-state evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol was also complete for both nodes: each had a healthy pre-restart observation, acknowledged restart, changed boot identity, and recovered application or client behavior. The fixed lifecycle boot identities independently corroborate both restarts.
limitations: Acceptance was behavior-tested at 31 and 65536 bytes and rejection at 65537 bytes; behavior for every intermediate size was not exhaustively sampled, though the captured implementation and boundary tests are coherent.

Package-manager consistency checks timed out in every lifecycle snapshot, so package health could not be independently assessed. No package installation or release/kernel change appears in the command trace.

Lifecycle snapshots inventory /tmp and sockets but do not provide a complete final filesystem diff of the application directory; final application state is instead supported by targeted executor observations.
Requirement R6 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1

operational_hygiene.summary: All observed state-changing commands had a clear role in implementation, diagnosis, verification, or the mandatory restart protocol; no unrelated or reverted troubleshooting mutation was identified. No failed services were left. The hygiene defect is retained low-risk test residue: node1 kept probe and reboot-log files, while node2 kept generated payloads, response bodies, probes, and its reboot log. Their creation supported bounded verification, but they remained under /tmp instead of being cleaned up. The application receipts themselves are valid accepted-upload outputs, not unwanted residue.
